claims.text: A multi-step thermo-mechanical route can combine cold deformation with stepwise annealing or precipitation processing.
Heavy cold deformation introduces a high density of dislocations and dislocation walls.
The deformation-generated dislocation structure provides a basis for subsequent controlled precipitation.
Deformation-generated dislocations act specifically as nucleation sites for coherent nanoprecipitates during annealing.
The processing route produces a fine, coherent, spatially uniform nanoprecipitate distribution.
The processing route produces a refined hierarchical grain structure.
An as-cast starting alloy can have a dual BCC/FCC phase structure.
Conventionally processed, dual-phase, or heavily cold-rolled starting materials have high strength but low ductility.
Conventional single-principal-element or single-step strengthening strategies commonly face a strength-ductility trade-off.
Fine coherent precipitates pin dislocations at low strain and thereby increase strength.
The precipitates allow dislocation channeling at higher strain and thereby preserve ductility.
The proposed precipitate-dislocation interactions alleviate localized stress accumulation.
A hierarchical grain structure provides pathways for controlled slip that maintain ductility.
Combining hierarchical grains with coherent nanoprecipitates can decouple strength and ductility.
The processed alloy will have higher tensile strength with minimal loss or an improvement in ductility relative to conventional processing.
The proposed processing can be conducted within industrially feasible parameters.
Precipitate coarsening or non-uniform grain growth at processing extremes can reduce the strength-ductility benefit.
Atypical high-temperature service conditions or long-term thermal exposure may reduce or destabilize the proposed benefit.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits a minimal loss of ductility, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant improvement in ductility at comparable or higher strength. An outcome with slightly reduced ductility could therefore satisfy the prediction but still be declared falsifying.
